claims.text: High-temperature oxidation resistance and long-term integrity in multiprincipal-element alloys are governed by the balance between reactive, fast-diffusing elements and slower-diffusing, high-oxygen-affinity elements.
Mn is a comparatively fast-diffusing reactive element under the relevant oxidation conditions.
V is a comparatively fast-diffusing reactive element under the relevant oxidation conditions.
Cr and Al are comparatively slow-diffusing, high-oxygen-affinity elements.
Mn promotes formation of nonprotective, porous oxides.
V promotes volatile or otherwise nonprotective oxides.
Cr and Al form continuous, dense, adherent protective Cr2O3 or Al2O3 scales.
Selective oxidation and surface segregation of constituent elements mediate whether a continuous passive oxide film forms.
Continuous Cr2O3 or Al2O3 scales act as diffusion barriers and slow oxygen ingress.
Mn- or V-bearing oxides can spall or generate porosity, thereby accelerating oxidation.
The relative diffusion rates and oxidation kinetics of the alloying elements determine overall oxidation behavior and retention of material integrity.
Increasing Cr and Al will produce slower oxidation, lower mass gain, thinner scales, and better scale adhesion than the baseline or Mn/V-enriched alloys.
Cr/Al-enriched alloys will tend toward parabolic oxidation kinetics.
Mn- or V-enriched alloys will exhibit faster, more nearly linear oxidation with porous scales and spallation.
The proposed governing behavior should apply from approximately 600 °C to 900 °C in oxidizing environments when phase stability and microstructure are comparable.
Secondary-phase formation, extensive grain growth, or non-oxidation degradation mechanisms can invalidate the proposed relationship.
The magnitude of the oxidation effect may depend on the alloy system and processing history.
A controlled test should compare protective-rich, reactive-rich, and intermediate-composition alloys while keeping processing and microstructure similar.
The comparison should use isothermal oxidation in air at about 800 °C for up to 100 hours.
Improved oxide-scale protection should result in improved post-oxidation mechanical-property retention.
